[07:00] Ethan: CPU can be viable for small models or quantized models. For 1536 dims on CPU, latency per embed is much higher and throughput lower. If cost is the only concern, you can offload batched offline vector generation to CPU and leave online low-latency requests on GPU. But for 1k QPS real-time, CPU might not be enough without a lot of machines.
[07:25] Sophie: For rerank — cross-encoder on GPU, how many qps can we expect?
[07:31] Ethan: Cross-encoder throughput depends on model size. A small cross-encoder distilled model can do maybe 50-200 pairwise evals/sec on a single GPU depending on batch. If you need 1k QPS and you rerank k=20 with a 100-pairs/sec card you'll need many cards — costy. Hence common pattern: keep ANN strong and only run cross-encoder on top 10-20 candidates or use a distilled light ranker.
[07:58] Clara: So let's run numbers: 1k QPS, k=20, cross-encoder pairs = 20k pair-evals/sec. If a GPU card can do 2k pair-evals/sec for the chosen model, we'd need 10 GPUs — expensive.
[08:20] Maya: Exactly — that's why many customers do bi-encoder + ANN to return top20 then a CPU light scorer or small transformer for rerank. Also caching helps if queries repeat.

[09:00] Ben: On the VPC/on-prem piece: can Redwood deploy the ANN index inside our VPC so data never leaves? Network latency inside VPC matters for egress between embedder and index.
[09:12] Samira: Yes, Redwood Private supports private control plane and data plane inside customer VPC. We can co-locate ANN storage nodes and inference nodes within the VPC; network hops between embed service and ANN storage are local, so you won't incur public egress.
[09:28] Ben: Great. How about storage sizing for 10M vectors at 1536 dims?
[09:32] Ethan: Rough calc: float32 1536 dims = 1536 * 4 bytes = 6144 bytes per vector ~6KB. 10M vectors ~60GB raw (actually ~61.4GB). But indexes add overhead: HNSW can be 2–4x memory overhead; with PQ you can drop to ~15–20GB. So plan for disk and RAM. Also replication for HA increases capacity.
[09:58] Sophie: So with PQ we might be able to fit in one big node?
[10:02] Ethan: Potentially, but for throughput and HA you'd likely distribute across multiple nodes. For example, 3-index shards each ~25GB. Also note that VA/OPQ requires offline conversion time.

[10:40] [12:00] (timestamp jumps in meeting due to rapid topics)
[12:15] Rajiv: Another trade: reducing dims from 1536 -> 768 halves storage (approx) and can speed ANN and reduce pairwise model size. But does it materially drop relevance? We saw small drops on some recall metrics.
[12:30] Maya: We recommend running AB tests: generate candidate recall and rerank delta for dims. That's why we asked for a repr dataset.

[13:00] Ethan: Quantization for embeddings is twofold: quantize stored vectors (PQ/OPQ) and quantize model weights (int8, fp16) for cheaper inference. Weight quantization is different: it may slightly change embedding quality. We run evals to see if quantized model preserves relative vector distances.
[13:26] Sophie: Did Redwood test 8-bit quantization for embedder weights on recall?
[13:31] Ethan: We have internal tests: for several open models int8 weight quantization usually has negligible effect on cosine-similarity ranking for many tasks but can be model dependent. We'll include bench results in follow up.

[14:00] Samira: Let's talk about batching numbers for ANN queries too. ANN queries can be batched on the index side to amortize CPU cost. If you get 1k qps, sending queries in micro-batches of 16–64 can increase throughput, but increases intra-query latency. For an SLO of 75ms, you'd want batching window <5ms.
[14:26] Ben: Our infra team prefers predictable p95 and low jitter — how does Redwood help with that?
[14:33] Maya: Redwood has per-route SLOs and can route low-latency traffic to hot nodes with smaller batch windows and higher cost to meet p95. We can also front-load caching of popular queries with prefix/KV cache to serve sub-10ms hits for repeat queries.

[15:10] Rajiv: About KV cache — can we prefetch reranked top results for frequently occurring queries?
[15:16] Ethan: Yes KV or prefix cache is good for top-N prefetch. For search, if top queries repeat, you can cache full top-10 result set and bypass ANN and cross-encoder entirely. Redwood supports TTL-based caches and hot-key promotion.

[16:00] Clara: A question about cost math for cross-encoder vs bi-encoder: can you give an example calc?
[16:07] Samira: Sure. Example rough numbers: bi-encoder embed cost per query (GPU) = $0.0002 (illustrative), ANN search cost (per query) = $0.00005, cross-encoder pair eval cost per pair = $0.0001. If k=10, cross-encoder cost per query = 10 * 0.0001 = $0.001. So total with cross-encoder = $0.00125 vs bi-encoder + ANN alone $0.00025. Order-of-magnitude difference. We'll provide real pricing later.

[17:00] Sophie: OK that math-ish is useful. We need to justify cross-encoder spend with relevance delta.
[17:08] Ethan: Exactly — quantify business lift per improved nDCG point. If the lift is significant, cross-encoder is worth it, else cheaper rerankers or cascade strategies are better.

[18:45] Ben: About quantization for ANN storage: when using PQ, is search latency impacted?
[18:52] Ethan: Typically PQ lowers memory bandwidth needs and can improve cache behavior, but introduces some decode cost per candidate — overall latency often improves but recall takes a hit. There are hybrid designs: store coarse vectors in PQ for candidate selection and keep a float shortlist for final exact re-ranking.

[20:00] [20:30] Rajiv: How do we benchmark at scale? We want to reproduce our production distribution and tail latencies.
[20:36] Ethan: Redwood suggests running bench with: real QPS pattern, cold start spikes, replica failover, and OF tests at scale. We supply a bench harness: you provide sample queries and ground truth; we run varying dims/batches and index configs (HNSW/IVF+PQ) and report p50/p95/p99 as well as recall/precision.

[22:10] Maya: We'll run multiple experiments: 1) 10M vectors, 1536 dims, HNSW no PQ; 2) 10M, 1536 dims, IVF+OPQ+PQ; 3) 10M, 768 dims. We'll capture recall@100 and end-to-end p95 with small reranker.

[24:00] Clara: For the PoC on-prem, what are the steps on infra side? Ben?
[24:06] Ben: We'll need a network diagram, port lists, instance types. We prefer minimal external dependencies and HSM/KMS integration.
[24:16] Samira: We'll send a network checklist and the security pack (SOC2/ISO) as action items. For HSM we integrate via customer KMS; we support bring-your-own-key for private deployments.

[26:00] [28:02] (Discussion on fallback strategies)
[28:10] Ethan: Also consider fallback models: if dedicated cross-encoder capacity is exhausted, fall back to smaller reranker or rely entirely on ANN results. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies per-route.

[30:00] Rajiv: On monitoring, can we get token-level cost & latency breakdown for rerank flows?
[30:07] Maya: Yes Redwood Console provides per-route trace, token and op-level cost breakdowns, and per-model p50/p95 with trace ids. We'll enable tracing in the PoC.

[32:00] Sophie: A modeling question: If we reduce dims, downstream cross-encoder might lose signal; have you tried projecting higher dims to lower dims with a small trainable adapter?
[32:10] Ethan: Yes a projection layer (learned PCA or small autoencoder) can map 1536->768 preserving task-specific info. That adds a small inference step but can reduce storage and speed up ANN. It's a valid engineering trade. We can test this in bench.

[34:00] Clara: Regarding index maintenance: how often should we rebuild indexes with PQ/OPQ?
[34:05] Ethan: OPQ requires an offline training period; for mostly static corpora you can offline rebuild nightly or weekly. For streaming updates, use incremental indexing for HNSW; periodic re-OPQ can be scheduled during low traffic.

[36:00] Ben: Any gotchas for on-prem GPUs and driver versions?
[36:05] Maya: Ensure libcudnn/cu* compat, and that our runtime's kernel selection matches your GPU arch. We'll provide a compatibility matrix. Also ensure NVMe throughput for index shards if not in RAM.

[38:20] [40:00] (Short break window in call — housekeeping)
[40:15] Samira: Quick recap: Bench design, cost spreadsheet, PoC schedule.

[41:00] Rajiv: I want to zero in on latency SLOs. We asked for p95 <75ms. Is that end-to-end including network, embed time, ANN time, reranker?
[41:09] Ethan: Yes end-to-end. It's tight but achievable with a hybrid approach: keep embed generation <20ms, ANN <10–20ms, reranker p95 <30ms (or small k), and network under 10ms inside VPC. That requires optimized batching, hot nodes and possibly smaller reranker.

[42:30] Sophie: If we cache popular queries, we can get p95 down to <10ms for those.

[44:00] Clara: What's Redwood's recommendation for k?
[44:05] Ethan: Start with k=20 for recall, measure recall@20 vs recall@100 and rerank delta. Often you can push k down to 10 with strong embedder + OPQ tuned. For cost-sensitive flows go lower.

[46:00] Rajiv: Any rough cost estimate for Dedicated capacity to handle 1k QPS and cross-encoder for top20?
[46:08] Samira: We'll run exact numbers but order magnitude: if you needed 10 GPUs for cross-encoder plus 1-2 GPUs for embed and index serving, plus infra, that's the expensive case. With a distilled reranker or smaller k you can reduce to ~2–3 GPUs. We'll model this in a sheet.

[48:00] Ben: For PII concerns, do embed vectors count as PII? We need guidance since it's financial text.
[48:06] Maya: Depends; embeddings can be reversible in theory. For regulated data you should apply data governance: encrypt at rest with KMS, limit retention, and possibly apply irreversible transforms if needed. We'll include compliance notes.

[50:10] Sophie: A practical question — for the bench, what metrics will we get?
[50:15] Ethan: p50/p95/p99 latency, QPS, recall@k, nDCG, memory/disk usage, GPU utilization, cost per query, tail jitter, failed queries. We'll correlate recall with index config.

[52:00] Rajiv: Also show how batch size affects tail latency — and continuous batching behavior.

[54:00] Samira: We'll simulate production QPS patterns including spikes to 1.5k and include failure scenarios.

[56:20] Clara: Are there any easy wins to start with?
[56:25] Ethan: Yes: 1) try 768-d embeddings to see recall drop, 2) enable OPQ+PQ with a small float shortlist for final rerank, 3) use a distilled lightweight reranker instead of full cross-encoder, 4) cache hot queries. These often reduce cost 2–5x.

[58:00] Rajiv: Ok, timeline — can Redwood run the bench next week?
[58:06] Samira: We can start the bench as soon as we get sample data. We'll aim to deliver bench results and a cost model within 5 business days after data receipt.

[59:30] Ben: One more infra question: network egress and private endpoints — is there a connector for on-prem HSM?
[59:36] Maya: Yes we support customer KMS via secure peering and can integrate with on-prem HSM via certified connectors; we'll share the integration doc.

[61:00] [62:00] (Wrap up technical clarifications)
[62:10] Sophie: Thank you — this is helpful. Please include sample graphs of recall vs dims and cost per QPS in the follow-up.

[64:00] Samira: Recap and next steps: 1) Rajiv sends sample queries + embed dump; 2) Ethan runs bench (dims/batches/index configs); 3) Samira shares pricing and security docs; 4) schedule PoC week.

[66:00] Clara: We'll target week of Mar 3 for PoC kickoff.

[68:00] Samira: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the sheet and bench plan.

[70:00] (Meeting ends)

End of transcript.
